title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: Behind every consolidated income statement is a physical product moving off a press or a furnace to solve a specific customer engineering problem.
epigraph.author: Philip Fisher — Scuttlebutt Manufacturing Lens

web_blocks.title: Anatomy of the Wheel Portfolio: Steel vs. Alloy and New Lightweighting Components

web_blocks.html: At first glance, SSWL looks like a single-product company: it makes wheels. Look closer at the factory floor, however, and you will find two fundamentally different manufacturing businesses—stamped steel rims and cast aluminium alloy wheels—plus an emerging precision-cast suspension business in aluminium steering knuckles [2][10][15]. In FY25, steel wheels generated roughly 68% to 69% of consolidated revenue, while aluminium alloy wheels contributed roughly 32% (on ~3.33 million alloy wheels sold) [10]. By FY26 and H1 FY27, alloy's contribution climbed further toward the 35%–45% band as Mehsana and Bhuj ramped up and management deliberately walked away from low-margin legacy passenger-car steel wheel contracts [10][24]. Consolidated sales reached ₹5,183 Cr in FY26 and ₹6,235 Cr on a trailing twelve-month (TTM) basis through September 2026 [1].

Why does the split between steel and alloy matter so much to you? Because a stamped steel wheel is a high-volume, thin-margin conversion business, whereas a low-pressure die-cast (LPDC) aluminium alloy wheel carries roughly three to four times higher realization per unit and substantially higher EBITDA per wheel [10][14]. Across the overall portfolio, SSWL's EBITDA per wheel expanded from ₹242 in prior comparable periods to ₹404 in recent reporting, driven by alloy mix, commercial vehicle recovery, and exports [14]. To see how the cash engine actually works, let us walk through each segment end to end with a concrete real-world customer example.

web_blocks.title: Segment 1: Passenger Vehicle Alloy Wheels — The Premiumization Engine

web_blocks.html: Consider a concrete end-to-end example of how SSWL wins and delivers an alloy wheel program. Take an Indian SUV maker such as Mahindra & Mahindra or Tata Motors launching a mid-tier electric or internal-combustion SUV. The automaker's engineering problem is dual: buyers increasingly demand diamond-cut, multi-spoke aesthetics even on mid-level trims, while vehicle engineers must shave unsprung rotational weight to meet range and fuel-economy targets [10][24]. SSWL's design team at Mehsana co-engineers the wheel geometry using finite-element impact and radial-fatigue simulations [2]. Once validated, molten A356 aluminium alloy is injected upward into precision steel dies using Low Pressure Die Casting (LPDC), minimizing porosity [2]. Each casting undergoes X-ray inspection, heat treatment, CNC diamond-cut machining, and multi-coat powder painting before being sequenced to the OEM assembly line [2]. Pricing is structured as a conversion fee plus a trailing three-month aluminium index pass-through, shielding SSWL from raw-metal spikes over an annual cycle [16].

web_blocks.title: Segment 2: Commercial Vehicle Steel Wheels — The Heavy-Duty Backbone

web_blocks.html: Now walk across to Jamshedpur, where SSWL commands roughly 54% of India's M&HCV steel wheel market and supplies 53% to 60% of Tata Motors' wheel requirements alongside 64% to 65% of Ashok Leyland's [11]. Here, the customer is a commercial truck OEM building 35-tonne to 55-tonne tractor-trailers for highway freight. The engineering problem is not styling; it is structural load endurance under overloaded Indian road conditions without adding dead weight that eats into payload. SSWL procures high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) hot-rolled steel coils directly from neighbouring Tata Steel, profiles the rim band through roll-forming and flash-butt welding, forms the heavy centre disc on hydraulic presses, joins them via submerged-arc welding, and applies cathodic electro-deposition (CED) primer [2][25]. Pricing follows a quarterly steel pass-through formula, meaning SSWL earns a stable conversion spread per kilogram or per wheel while carrying the working-capital float between coil purchase and OEM collection [16].

web_blocks.title: Segment 3: Tractors, OTR, and 2W/3W Steel Wheels — Rural & EV Niches

web_blocks.html: In tractors and off-the-road (OTR) equipment—where SSWL holds ~42% domestic market share—a tractor manufacturer such as Mahindra Farm Equipment needs deep-dish, heavy-gauge rear wheels capable of surviving high-torque mud traction and ballasted ploughing [11]. SSWL manufactures these thick-section rims at Dappar and Bhuj, where lower competitive intensity yields healthier spreads than commodity car steel wheels [10][25]. Meanwhile, in two- and three-wheelers, the growth catalyst has shifted to electric scooters and e-rickshaws. An Indian EV two-wheeler OEM requires custom-stamped steel wheels engineered to house rear hub motors and withstand higher instant torque; SSWL's high-speed stamping lines deliver these at scale, allowing the 2W/3W segment to outpace broader domestic industry volumes [10].

web_blocks.title: Segment 4: Aluminium Steering Knuckles — Beyond the Wheel

web_blocks.html: SSWL's newest segment moves inboard from the wheel rim to the suspension upright. An automotive steering knuckle connects the wheel hub, brake caliper, and suspension strut. Traditionally made from heavy cast iron, modern EVs and SUVs are switching to cast aluminium knuckles to cut unsprung weight by 40% to 50% and improve steering responsiveness [15][27]. Previously, Indian OEMs imported these safety-critical castings. SSWL commissioned an initial 0.5 million to 0.6 million unit line—ramping to 85%–90% utilization—and is adding another 1 million units in Gujarat [15][27]. For an EV platform like Mahindra's born-electric SUVs, SSWL casts, heat-treats, and CNC-machines the knuckle to micron-level bearing tolerances, pricing it on a specialized casting-plus-machining contract that mirrors its alloy wheel playbook [15].

web_blocks.title: Segment 5: Global Exports (US & EU) — The High-Margin Counterweight

web_blocks.html: Exports generated ₹561 Cr in FY25—split 64% to the United States and 32% to the European Union—and continued scaling in FY26 and H1 FY27 [10]. Consider a North American trailer or OTR distributor seeking alternatives to Chinese steel wheels hit by U.S. Section 232 tariffs and anti-dumping duties [23]. SSWL manufactures TUV-certified steel trailer wheels and aftermarket/OEM alloy wheels in Chennai and Mehsana, packs them into ocean containers, and ships them under multi-year supply agreements [2][10]. Export wheels carry higher EBITDA per unit than domestic OEM steel wheels, though they expose SSWL to longer ocean-transit inventory cycles and U.S./EU trade-policy shifts [14][23].

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Why Product Mix Drives the Entire P&L
paragraphs: If you treat SSWL as a generic auto-ancillary maker, you miss the real story. Walking away from low-margin passenger car steel wheels while doubling down on alloy wheels, aluminium knuckles, and US/EU trailer and alloy exports is why EBITDA per wheel jumped from ₹242 to ₹404.

Every percentage point of revenue that shifts from a commodity stamped steel rim into an LPDC alloy wheel or a CNC-machined steering knuckle raises the profit earned per ton of factory floor space—provided the plants stay above 75%–80% utilization.

book_paragraphs: At first glance, Steel Strips Wheels looks like a single-product manufacturer: it makes wheels. Step onto the shop floor, however, and you will see two distinct industrial businesses—stamped steel rims and cast aluminium alloy wheels—alongside a fast-scaling precision-cast suspension business in aluminium steering knuckles. In FY25, steel wheels accounted for roughly 68% to 69% of consolidated revenue, while alloy wheels contributed roughly 32% on 3.33 million units sold. By FY26 and the first half of FY27, alloy's share pushed higher as Mehsana and Bhuj ramped up and management deliberately exited low-margin passenger-car steel wheel contracts. Consolidated sales climbed to ₹5,183 Cr in FY26 and ₹6,235 Cr on a trailing twelve-month basis through September 2026.

Why does this mix shift matter so much to an owner? A stamped steel wheel is a high-volume, thin-margin metal-bending business, whereas a low-pressure die-cast aluminium alloy wheel commands three to four times higher realization per wheel and materially higher EBITDA per unit. Across the company, EBITDA per wheel expanded from ₹242 in prior periods to ₹404 recently. To understand how SSWL earns that spread, let us trace each segment through a concrete customer transaction.

book_subsections.title: Passenger Vehicle Alloy Wheels and Commercial Vehicle Steel Wheels
paragraphs: Take a passenger vehicle alloy wheel program for an Indian SUV maker such as Mahindra or Tata Motors. Buyers increasingly expect diamond-cut alloy wheels even on mid-level trims, while engineers need lower unsprung rotational weight to protect EV range and fuel economy. SSWL's engineers at Mehsana co-design the wheel using finite-element fatigue simulations. Molten A356 aluminium is then injected upward into precision dies via Low Pressure Die Casting to eliminate air pockets. Each wheel goes through X-ray screening, heat treatment, CNC diamond-cut machining, and multi-coat painting before sequenced delivery. Pricing is structured as a conversion fee plus a trailing three-month aluminium index pass-through.

Now walk over to Jamshedpur, where SSWL holds roughly 54% of India's medium and heavy commercial vehicle steel wheel market and supplies 53% to 60% of Tata Motors' requirements alongside 64% to 65% of Ashok Leyland's. A truck maker building 35-tonne to 55-tonne highway haulers needs rims that survive overloaded Indian roads without excess dead weight. SSWL buys high-strength low-alloy steel coils from neighbouring Tata Steel, roll-forms and flash-butt welds the rim band, presses the heavy centre disc, welds the assembly, and applies cathodic electro-deposition primer. Pricing follows a quarterly steel pass-through, leaving SSWL with a steady conversion margin while it finances the working-capital cycle.

book_subsections.title: Tractors, Two-Wheelers, Aluminium Knuckles, and Global Exports
paragraphs: In tractors and off-the-road equipment—where SSWL commands roughly 42% domestic share—farm OEMs require deep-dish, heavy-gauge rear wheels built for high-torque mud traction. Produced at Dappar and Bhuj, these thick-section wheels face fewer competitors and earn healthier spreads than commodity car steel rims. In two- and three-wheelers, growth has pivoted toward electric scooters and e-rickshaws that require custom-stamped wheels engineered around rear hub motors.

SSWL's newest product line moves inboard to the suspension upright: aluminium steering knuckles. Replacing heavy cast-iron knuckles with cast aluminium cuts unsprung weight by 40% to 50% for EVs and modern SUVs, serving as direct import substitution for Indian OEMs. After scaling its initial 0.5 million to 0.6 million unit line to 85%–90% utilization, SSWL is adding another 1 million units in Gujarat. Finally, exports—which reached ₹561 Cr in FY25, split 64% to the U.S. and 32% to the European Union—supply TUV-certified trailer, OTR, and alloy wheels to Western buyers seeking alternatives to tariff-hit Chinese imports. Export orders carry superior EBITDA per wheel, though they lengthen ocean-transit inventory cycles and introduce trade-policy sensitivity.

Stepping back, notice how these five segments reinforce one another inside a single OEM relationship. When SSWL supplies a Mahindra or Tata Motors platform, it can now pitch stamped steel wheels for base trims, diamond-cut LPDC alloy wheels for upper trims, and cast aluminium steering knuckles for the underlying EV or SUV chassis. That cross-selling lowers customer acquisition friction while lifting revenue per vehicle. At the same time, steel wheels for commercial trucks (~54% market share) and tractors (~42% market share) keep base tonnage humming through the presses, while export containers to North America and Europe absorb capacity whenever domestic passenger-car demand pauses.
